finding.title: Deferred serialization reads the buffer after flush empties it, so every audit batch is written as an empty string

findings.title: Deferred serialization reads the buffer after flush empties it, so every audit batch is written as an empty string
findings.scenario: After 20 recordAudit calls, EventBuffer.flush calls this.write(this.items). write only queues the .then callback, then flush runs this.items.length = 0 synchronously on the same array. When the callback runs, events is empty, so appendFile writes ''. The same happens in flushAudit on close. Every audit event is lost, the file stays empty, and no error is logged.
findings.whyNotPrevented: EventBuffer.flush passes its live array and clears it straight after write returns, which was only safe while the write was synchronous. Emptying the array raises no error, so onError never fires, and the repo has no tests. Fix by serializing synchronously in write, before queueing, or by having EventBuffer hand off a copy or a fresh array.

findings.title: A failed background write permanently drops the batch and only logs it
findings.scenario: The disk is briefly full, or the audit file is unwritable, when a batch is flushed, so appendFile rejects with ENOSPC or EACCES. The old appendFileSync threw before items.length = 0, so the events stayed in the buffer and were retried on the next add. Now the batch has already been cleared, onError logs to console.error, and those audit records are gone. flushAudit also resolves normally on close, so shutdown reports success after losing events.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The catch swallows the rejection so the chain keeps going, and writer.idle() therefore always resolves. No retry or re-queue exists, no caller passes an onError that could react, and no test covers a failed write.

finding.title: Batch is serialized after EventBuffer has cleared the array, so audit events are lost

findings.title: Batch is serialized after EventBuffer has cleared the array, so audit events are lost
findings.scenario: The 20th recordAudit call triggers EventBuffer.flush(), which calls this.write(this.items) and then runs this.items.length = 0 synchronously. The .then callback runs later and maps the same array, which is now empty, so appendFile writes '' and all 20 events are lost. The same happens to the final batch in flushAudit. If an earlier append is still in flight, the callback instead sees whatever newer events are in the array at that moment. Those events are written early, out of order, and can be written again by the next batch, while the original batch is still lost.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The old appendFileSync call read the array before flush cleared it, so reusing the array was safe. The deferred callback breaks that assumption. The array is passed by reference with no copy, and the repository has no tests.

findings.title: A failed append permanently drops the batch and flushAudit still resolves
findings.scenario: The audit disk is full or the file is temporarily unwritable (ENOSPC or EACCES) when a batch is written. appendFile rejects and onError logs only the error, not the events, then the chain continues. EventBuffer has already cleared the batch, so those audit records are gone even if the disk recovers. During shutdown, flushAudit resolves normally, so onClose sees success. Before this change, appendFileSync threw before this.items.length = 0, so the events stayed buffered for the next flush and the failure reached the caller.
findings.whyNotPrevented: write() now always returns synchronously without an error, so EventBuffer's clear-after-write ordering no longer protects the events. idle() resolves because .catch swallows the rejection. No caller passes a custom onError, and the repository has no tests for write failures.

findings.scenario: If appendFile fails with ENOSPC or EACCES, the default onError logs only the error and the batch's events are discarded without a retry or a record of what was lost. During shutdown, flushAudit resolves normally, so the onClose caller cannot tell that audit records were lost.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The catch is needed to keep the chain alive after a failure, but it does not pass the failed events to onError. idle() also never reports that a failure occurred, and no caller passes a custom onError.

finding.title: Omitted flags overwrite the defaults with undefined, so the probe fails

findings.title: Omitted flags overwrite the defaults with undefined, so the probe fails
findings.scenario: Running status-probe with no flags makes cli.js pass { baseUrl: undefined, retries: undefined, timeoutMs: undefined }. Object spread copies undefined values, so config.retries is undefined. `0 <= undefined` is false, the loop never runs, no request is sent, and get() runs `throw lastError` with undefined. Passing only --retries 1 leaves baseUrl and timeoutMs undefined, so that run fails too: AbortSignal.timeout(undefined) is expected to throw inside the try, and the request URL would start with 'undefined/status'. Every run that omits a flag loses that flag's default, which breaks the stated goal of keeping defaults.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The repo has no tests and no type checking. cli.js is the only caller of createClient, and it always passes all three keys, so the failure happens on every run that omits a flag.

findings.title: Invalid --retries and --timeout values are not validated
findings.scenario: --retries abc gives NaN and --retries -1 gives -1. In both cases the `attempt <= config.retries` check is false on the first pass, so no request is sent and get() throws undefined, with no message naming the bad flag. --retries Infinity against an unreachable host retries forever. --timeout abc gives NaN, which AbortSignal.timeout is expected to reject inside the try block, so the error is retried and then surfaces as an unrelated range error rather than a bad-flag message.
findings.whyNotPrevented: parseArgs with type 'string' accepts any text, Number() returns NaN rather than throwing, and neither cli.js nor createClient checks the result. Fixing the undefined-default bug does not help, because NaN and -1 are not undefined.

finding.title: Entries at exactly UTC midnight are counted in two days, so renewals are double-counted

other.title: No upper limit on the report range, so one request can block the server

findings.title: Entries at exactly UTC midnight are counted in two days, so renewals are double-counted
findings.scenario: `Ledger.entriesBetween` includes both ends (`entry.at <= to`), and `chargeRenewal` always records `at: startOfDay(periodStart)`, which is exactly midnight. A 1000-cent renewal at 2026-03-02T00:00:00Z with from=2026-03-01&to=2026-03-04 appears in the 03-01 row and the 03-02 row. The report gives totalCents 2000 instead of 1000, and the 03-01 row shows 1000 where `dayStatement` for that day shows 0. With from=2026-03-01&to=2026-03-02, the same renewal is counted in 03-01 even though it falls on the excluded end date. Fix: end each day at `endOfDay(day)`, as `dayStatement` does at src/statement.js:5, or reuse that per-day total.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The existing caller, `dayStatement`, avoids this by passing `endOfDay` (the last millisecond of the day). The new code passes the next midnight instead. Nothing in `entriesBetween` signals the inclusive upper bound, and the repository has no tests.

findings.title: No upper limit on the report range, so one request can block the server
findings.scenario: A mistyped year such as from=0202-01-01&to=2026-01-01 passes validation and runs about 666,000 loop iterations. Each iteration calls `entriesBetween`, which filters the whole ledger, so 10,000 entries means about 6.7 billion filter checks in one synchronous handler. The process cannot serve other requests until it finishes, and the response holds hundreds of thousands of rows.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The route checks only that the dates parse and that from is before to. `dailyRevenue` loops synchronously over every day and rescans all entries each time, and nothing in the repository limits the range or the request time.

findings.title: The `to` date is silently excluded from the report
findings.quote: for (let day = startOfDay(from); day < to; day = addDays(day, 1)) {
findings.scenario: from=2026-01-01&to=2026-01-31 returns 30 rows with no row for Jan 31, and from=to returns 400, so a one-day report needs to set to the following day. A caller who reads the range as inclusive under-reports revenue with no warning. If exclusive is intended, the error message and route should say so.

findings.title: Charges at exactly UTC midnight are counted in two days and double-counted in the range total
findings.scenario: A 999-cent renewal is recorded at 2026-03-02T00:00:00Z, and chargeRenewal always records at startOfDay. With from=2026-03-01&to=2026-03-03, the rows are 03-01: 999 and 03-02: 999, and totalCents is 1998. The correct rows are 0 and 999, with a total of 999. With to=2026-03-02, the charge falls after the requested range but still appears under 03-01. Every renewal is at midnight, so any renewal that falls on a boundary between rows, or on the to date, is misreported.
findings.whyNotPrevented: Ledger.entriesBetween is inclusive at both ends (entry.at <= to), so the next day's midnight matches both days. dayStatement avoids this by passing endOfDay(day), but this code passes addDays(day, 1). The repo has no tests, and nothing in the types or the code rejects overlapping windows. Fix: pass endOfDay(day) as the upper bound and add a test with a renewal at midnight.

findings.title: Revenue report has no limit on range size, so one request can block the server
findings.scenario: GET /reports/revenue?from=0001-01-01&to=9999-12-31 passes validation. dailyRevenue then runs about 3.65 million synchronous iterations, each filtering the whole ledger, and builds a row for every day. With a 100k-entry ledger that is about 3.6e11 comparisons, which blocks the handler and all other requests and produces a huge response.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The route only checks that the dates parse and that from is before to. dailyRevenue has no cap, and entriesBetween scans all entries on every call. Fix options are to cap the range length with a 400, or to scan the ledger once and bucket entries by day.

findings.scenario: from=2026-03-01&to=2026-03-31 returns no row for 03-31, and that day's revenue is missing from the total. from=2026-03-01&to=2026-03-01 returns 400. The error message says only that from must be before to, and nothing documents that to is exclusive.

finding.title: Rate-limit key uses the raw email, so changing case or whitespace bypasses the limit

other.title: Client-chosen login keys grow the limiter map without bound
Login rate limiting has no tests

findings.title: Rate-limit key uses the raw email, so changing case or whitespace bypasses the limit
findings.scenario: An attacker sends guesses for victim@example.com as 'Victim@example.com', 'VICTIM@example.com', ' victim@example.com', 'victim@example.com ' and so on. Each spelling gets its own limiter window and 5 attempts, but findByEmail normalizes them all to the same account. Whitespace padding gives unlimited variants, so password guessing is never limited. Separately, a successful login as 'Victim@example.com' does not clear the count stored under 'victim@example.com'.
findings.whyNotPrevented: Normalization happens only inside UserStore.findByEmail through normalizeEmail in src/emails.js, after the key is built. RateLimiter treats keys as opaque strings, and the repository has no tests that exercise login with email variants.

findings.title: Client-chosen login keys grow the limiter map without bound
findings.scenario: An unauthenticated client posts /login with a new random email on each request. Each request adds an entry to RateLimiter.windows before the user lookup. Those entries are never removed, because expired windows are replaced only when the same key returns and reset runs only after a successful login. Sustained traffic grows process memory until the server runs out of memory, which also clears all in-memory attempt counts if the process restarts.
findings.whyNotPrevented: RateLimiter has no eviction or size cap. Its existing use is keyed by request.ip, which limits the key space far more than arbitrary email strings do. /login has no per-IP limit, and nothing in the repository restricts the email's length or format before allow() runs.

findings.title: Login rate limiting has no tests
findings.scenario: Nothing checks that the sixth attempt returns 429, that a successful login clears the count, or that the window expires. A regression in any of these would go unnoticed.
findings.measuredBy: Glob "**/*" in the repository: no test files, and package.json has no test script

finding.title: Attempt limit is keyed on the raw email, so case or whitespace variants bypass it

findings.title: Attempt limit is keyed on the raw email, so case or whitespace variants bypass it
findings.scenario: After 5 wrong passwords for bob@example.com, the next attempt returns 429. An attacker then sends Bob@example.com, BOB@example.com, or ' bob@example.com'. Each variant gets a new 5-attempt counter, but findByEmail normalizes it to the same account and verifies the password. The attacker can keep guessing well past 5 attempts per 15 minutes, limited only by the number of variants. A successful login also clears only the counter for the spelling used, so counters for other spellings remain.
findings.whyNotPrevented: normalizeEmail is applied only inside UserStore, after the limiter key is built from the unnormalized input. The repository has no tests, so nothing checks that variants share a counter.
findings.measuredBy: Grep "normalizeEmail" in src: used only in src/users.js and defined in src/emails.js, not in src/login.js; Glob "**/*{test,spec}*": no files

findings.title: Unauthenticated login requests can grow the limiter map without bound
findings.scenario: A client posts /login with a different random email on each request. allow() runs before the user lookup, so each string adds a permanent Map entry, even when no such account exists. Expired entries are replaced only if the same key returns, and failed attempts never call reset. Sustained traffic therefore raises process memory until the API runs out of memory and crashes.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The only deletion path is reset(), which login calls only after a successful login. The new login limiter uses client-chosen strings as keys, /login has no per-IP limit, and RateLimiter has no expiry sweep or size cap.
findings.measuredBy: Grep "windows\.(delete|clear)" in src: only match is src/rate-limit.js:21 inside reset(); Grep "\.reset\(" in src: only caller is src/login.js:12 on successful login

finding.title: Rate-limit key uses the raw email, so changing its case or spacing bypasses the limit

other.title: Unauthenticated login requests can grow the limiter map without bound

findings.title: Rate-limit key uses the raw email, so changing its case or spacing bypasses the limit
findings.scenario: An attacker guesses passwords for victim@x.com. After 5 failures they send Victim@x.com, then VICTIM@x.com, then ' victim@x.com'. Each spelling gets a new limiter bucket with 5 more attempts, but findByEmail normalizes them all to the same account. Case and whitespace variants provide effectively unlimited guesses, so the limit of 5 per account is not enforced. A successful login with one spelling also clears only that spelling's count.
findings.whyNotPrevented: UserStore.findByEmail normalizes internally with normalizeEmail, but login builds the key from the unnormalized body.email. No route code normalizes the email first, and the repository has no tests. The key should use normalizeEmail(body.email).

findings.title: Unauthenticated login requests can grow the limiter map without bound
findings.scenario: An unauthenticated client POSTs /login with a different random email on each request, including addresses with no account and very long strings. Each request stores a new entry before the user lookup. Failed-login entries are never removed after their window expires, so memory grows until the process runs out and crashes.
findings.whyNotPrevented: RateLimiter only replaces an expired entry when the same key returns, and reset runs only after a successful login. This change also moves the key from the existing limiter's request.ip pattern to a value the client can choose freely, and nothing limits requests per IP or validates email length on /login.

findings.scenario: getUTCMonth is zero-based, so createdAt 2026-03-05 renders as 2026-02-05 on invoices, receipts, shipped emails, and as 2026/02/05 in the CSV. findings.scenario: A customerName of "North\rShop" is written unquoted because the pattern only looks for a quote, a comma or \n. Parsers that treat CR as a line ending split that order across two rows. Adding \r to the pattern fixes it.

findings.scenario: The 400 responses for missing, malformed or reversed dates are untested. So is the rule that orders on the to date are included, which depends on adding one day because listOrders uses an exclusive upper bound. A regression in any of these would pass npm test.

findings.title: Missing-account path throws before the try, so the lock is never released and the worker hangs
findings.quote: throw new PayoutError(`payout ${payoutId} has no bank account`);
findings.scenario: Payout 42 has no accountNumber. sendPayout acquires `payout:42`, marks it failed and throws outside the try, so release() never runs. The worker catches the error and calls job.retryLater(). When job 42 is redelivered, acquire() awaits a promise on the held entry that never resolves. runPayouts handles jobs one at a time, so that await stops all payouts in the process. The same leak now happens if payouts.get or payouts.update rejects, because the diff moved payouts.get out of the try, where a get failure used to release the lock.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The finally block only covers code inside the try, and the new code sits before it. acquire() has no timeout, and the repo has no test files.

findings.title: Permanent missing-account failure is retried instead of being finished
findings.scenario: A payout with no accountNumber makes sendPayout throw PayoutError. The worker's catch treats every error the same way, so the job is never acked and goes back through retryLater. Even with the lock leak fixed, each redelivery repeats the failed update, logs the error and requeues the job, so a payout already marked failed stays in the queue. The queue code is not in this repo, so any retry cap is unknown.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The catch in runPayouts does not distinguish PayoutError from transient errors, and the diff does not change worker.js. No test covers this path.

findings.title: Account check runs before the already-sent check and can mark a paid payout as failed
findings.scenario: A payout has { status: 'sent', transferId: 't1', accountNumber: null }, for example because the account was removed after payment, and its job is redelivered after job.ack() failed. The new check runs first and overwrites the status to 'failed', although the money was sent. The early return for 'sent' payouts is never reached, and the wrong status could prompt a second payment. Nothing in this repo shows whether accountNumber can be cleared after sending, because the payouts store is not here.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The diff places the new check ahead of the existing idempotency check, and nothing in the code or tests stops a sent payout from moving to failed.

findings.title: Refund moves money from the customer to the store
findings.scenario: Refunding a 1000-cent order for customer 'c1' calls transfer('store', 'c1', 1000). Since the signature is transfer(toAccountId, fromAccountId, amountCents), c1's balance drops by 1000 and the store's rises by 1000, so the customer is charged again instead of refunded.

The arguments look natural when read as from/to, but ledger.js takes the destination first, as payOutSeller does with transfer(seller.accountId, STORE_ACCOUNT, amountCents).

findings.title: Failed uploads now look successful, so the local archive is deleted
findings.quote: await retry(() => bucket.put(key, body, { contentType: 'application/x-ndjson' }), { attempts: 3, label: `upload ${key}` });
findings.scenario: If bucket.put rejects on all 3 attempts, retry (src/retry.js:10) does `return report(error, ...)`, which logs the error and resolves to undefined. uploadArchive then returns the key, and archiveDay (src/archive.js:9) runs unlink(file). That day's .ndjson file is deleted although it was never uploaded, so the report data is permanently lost. runNightly also pushes the key to `archived`, so the reports.archived metric counts the failed day as a success. Before this change, the rejection propagated, unlink was skipped and the file stayed on disk for a later run.
findings.whyNotPrevented: retry swallows the final error instead of rethrowing it, and uploadArchive ignores its return value. The catch in runNightly never fires because nothing throws. The repository has no test files, so no test covers exhausted retries.

findings.title: Retry window of about 600ms is too short to ride out a storage outage
findings.quote: await retry(() => bucket.put(key, body, { contentType: 'application/x-ndjson' }), { attempts: 3, label: `upload ${key}` });
findings.scenario: The call uses the default delayMs of 200, so retry waits 200ms after attempt 1 and 400ms after attempt 2 (`delayMs * attempt`, src/retry.js:11). With fast-failing connections, a storage outage lasting 5 seconds fails all 3 attempts within about 600ms, and the nightly upload fails despite the retries. The stated goal of surviving a brief outage is met only for blips shorter than about a second.
findings.whyNotPrevented: uploadArchive passes no delayMs, so it inherits a default that nothing tunes for storage outages. No test or configuration sets a minimum retry window.

findings.title: Slow older search responses overwrite newer results
findings.scenario: The user types 'sho', pauses for over 200ms, then types 'shoes'. If the 'sho' response arrives after the 'shoes' response, the list shows 'sho' results while the input says 'shoes'. Similarly, if the user deletes 'ab' down to 'a' while the 'ab' request is in flight, the list is cleared and then refilled with 'ab' results.
findings.whyNotPrevented: debounce only cancels timers that have not fired, not requests already in flight. searchProducts takes no abort signal, and nothing checks that term still matches the input before renderResults runs. The repo has no tests for this path.

findings.title: Pressing Enter no longer searches
findings.scenario: If the input is prefilled by browser form restoration or by code, no input event fires, so pressing Enter does nothing and no results appear. Likewise, after a search fails, pressing Enter cannot retry it; the user has to change the text.

findings.title: One-character searches are no longer possible

findings.title: Saved preferences overwrite the shared defaults and leak between users
findings.scenario: User A has savedPreferences {"theme":"dark"} and user B has null. getUser(A) writes theme='dark' into the DEFAULT_PREFERENCES singleton, because defaultPreferences() returns that object rather than a copy. getUser(B) then returns theme 'dark' instead of 'light'. The change lasts for the life of the process, so every later user without a saved theme gets A's value, and responses depend on request order.
findings.whyNotPrevented: defaultPreferences() in src/defaults.js line 8 returns the module-level object, which is not frozen or cloned, and its name suggests a fresh value. The repository has no tests, so nothing exercises two users in sequence.

findings.title: The `in` check accepts inherited keys, so some unsupported saved keys are not ignored
findings.scenario: savedPreferences {"constructor":"x"} or {"toString":"x"} passes the check because `in` walks the prototype chain, so the response includes an unsupported key. A saved JSON key "__proto__" also passes: JSON.parse makes it an own key, and the assignment then replaces the prototype of the preferences object, which is the shared defaults object while the first finding stands.
findings.whyNotPrevented: saveUser stores savedPreferences without validating keys, loadUser returns them as parsed, and no test covers keys that match Object.prototype members. Object.hasOwn(preferences, key) would limit the check to supported keys.

findings.title: The `in` check lets inherited property names through as supported keys
findings.scenario: With savedPreferences {"constructor":"x"} or {"toString":"x"}, `key in preferences` is true through Object.prototype, so the unsupported key is copied and returned in the response instead of being ignored. A saved own "__proto__" key from JSON.parse also passes, and the assignment replaces the prototype of the object, which is currently the shared defaults object.
findings.whyNotPrevented: `in` walks the prototype chain, and saveUser stores savedPreferences without validating keys. Nothing else filters keys before this loop, and no test covers it. Object.hasOwn(preferences, key) would check only the supported keys.
